title: Chapter 119 — The Candles
paragraphs: Warmest climates but nurse the cruellest fangs: the tiger of Bengal crouches in spiced groves of ceaseless verdure. Skies the most brilliant but basket the deadliest thunders: gorgeous Cuba knows tornadoes that never swept tame northern lands. So too it is that in these resplendent Japanese seas the mariner encounters the deadliest typhoons.

Toward evening of that day, the Pequod was torn of her canvas and, bare-poled, was left to fight a typhoon which had struck her directly ahead. When darkness came on, sky and sea roared and split with the thunder and blazed with the lightning that showed the disabled masts fluttering here and there with the rags which the first fury of the storm had left for its after-sport.

Holding by a shroud, Starbuck was standing on the quarter-deck; at every flash of lightning glancing aloft to see what additional disaster might have befallen the intricate rigging there; while Stubb and Flask were directing the men in the higher hoisting and firmer lashing of the boats. But all their efforts seemed in vain.

"Bad work, bad work! Mr. Starbuck," said Stubb, regarding the wreck, "but the sea will have its way. Stubb, for one, can't fight it. You see, Mr. Starbuck, a wave has such a great long start before it leaps, all round the world it runs, and then comes the spring! But as for me, all the start I have to begin with is just across this deck here. And a pull or a jolt or a sail torn, is my signal to spring — that's all."
Oh! jolly is the gale, / And a joker is the whale, / A-flourishing his tail — / Such a funny, sporty, gamy, jesty, joky, hoky-poky lad, is the Ocean, oh!
The scud all a-flying, / That's his flip only foaming; / When he stirs in the spicing — / Such a funny, sporty, gamy, jesty, joky, hoky-poky lad, is the Ocean, oh!
Thunder splits the ships, / But he only smacks his lips, / A-tasting of this flip — / Such a funny, sporty, gamy, jesty, joky, hoky-poky lad, is the Ocean, oh!
"Enough, Stubb," cried Starbuck, "let the Typhoon sing, and strike his harp here in our rigging; but if you are a brave man you will hold your peace."

"But I am not a brave man; never said I was a brave man; I am a coward; and I sing to keep up my spirits. And I tell you what it is, Mr. Starbuck, there's no way to stop my singing in this world but to cut my throat. And when that's done, ten to one I sing you the doxology for a wind-up."
"Madman! Look through my eyes if you have none of your own."
"What! How can you see better on a dark night than anybody else, never mind how foolish?"

"Here!" cried Starbuck, seizing Stubb by the shoulder and pointing his hand toward the weather bow, "mark you not that the gale comes from the eastward, the very course Ahab is to run for Moby Dick? The very course he swung to this day at noon? Now mark his boat there; where is that stove? In the stern-sheets, man — where he is wont to stand. His very body was there but an hour ago. I saw him then. The boat's whole bottom is stove in!"
"I don't half understand you; what's in the wind?"

"Yes, yes, round the Cape of Good Hope is the shortest way to Nantucket," mused Starbuck suddenly, paying no attention to Stubb's question. "The gale that now hammers at us to stave us, we can turn it into a fair wind that will drive us toward home. Over there, to windward, all is blackness of doom; but to leeward, homeward — I see it lightens up there; but not with the lightning."
At that moment in one of the intervals of profound darkness following the flashes, a voice was heard at his side; and almost at the same instant a volley of thunder peals rolled overhead.
"Who's there?"
"Old Thunder!" said Ahab, groping his way along the bulwarks to his pivot-hole; but suddenly finding his path made plain by angled lances of fire.

Now, as the lightning rod to a spire on shore is intended to carry off the dangerous fluid into the soil, so the similar rod which at sea some ships carry to each mast is intended to conduct it into the water. But as this conductor must descend to considerable depth, so that its end may avoid all contact with the hull, the lower end was left trailing in the sea until the storm came. It was then hauled up alongside.

"The rods! The rods!" cried Starbuck to the crew, suddenly alerted by the vivid lightning that had just been darting flamelike, to light Ahab to his post. "Are they overboard? Drop them over, fore and aft. Quick!"

"Stop!" cried Ahab; "let's have fair play here, though we be the weaker side. Yet I'll contribute to raise rods on the Himalayas and Andes, that all the world may be secured; but away with privileges! Let them be, sir."
"Look aloft!" cried Starbuck. "The corpusants! The corpusants!"

All the yard-arms were tipped with a pallid fire; and touched at each three-pointed lightning-rod-end with three tapering white flames, each of the three tall masts was silently burning in that sulfurous air, like three gigantic wax tapers before an altar.

"Blast the boat! Let it go!" cried Stubb at this instant, as a washing sea heaved up under his own little craft, so that its gunwale violently jammed his hand as he was passing a lashing. "Blast it!" But slipping backward on the deck, his uplifted eyes caught the flames; and immediately shifting his tone, he cried: "The corpusants have mercy on us all!"

To sailors, oaths are everyday words; they will swear in the trance of the calm and in the teeth of the tempest; they will hurl curses from the topsail-yard-arms when most they teeter over a seething sea; but in all my voyaging, seldom have I heard a common oath when God's burning finger has been laid on the ship — when His Mene, Mene, Tekel, Upharsin has been woven into the shrouds and the cordage.

While this pallidness was burning aloft, few words were heard from the enchanted crew; who in one thick cluster stood on the forecastle, all their eyes gleaming in that pale phosphorescence, like a far-away constellation of stars. Relieved against the ghostly light, the gigantic jet-black negro, Daggoo, loomed up to thrice his real stature, and seemed the black cloud from which the thunder had come. The parted mouth of Tashtego revealed his shark-white teeth, which strangely gleamed as if they too had been tipped by corpusants; while lit up by the preternatural light, Queequeg's tattooing burned like Satanic blue flames on his body.

The tableau all waned at last with the pallidness aloft; and once more the Pequod and every soul on her decks were wrapped in a pall. A moment or two passed, when Starbuck, going forward, pushed against someone. It was Stubb. "What do you think now, man; I heard your cry; it was not the same in the song."

"No, no, it wasn't; I said the corpusants have mercy on us all; and I hope they will, still. But do they only have mercy on long faces? Have they no sympathy for a laugh? And look, Mr. Starbuck — but it's too dark to look. Hear me, then: I take that mast-head flame we saw for a sign of good luck; for those masts are rooted in a hold that is going to be chock-full of sperm-oil, d'you see; and so, all that sperm will work up into the masts, like sap in a tree. Yes, our three masts will yet be as three sperm candles — that's the good promise we saw."

At that moment Starbuck caught sight of Stubb's face slowly beginning to glimmer into view. Glancing upward, he cried: "See! See!" And once more the high tapering flames were beheld with what seemed redoubled otherworldliness in their pallor.
"The corpusants have mercy on us all," cried Stubb again.

At the base of the mainmast, full beneath the doubloon and the flame, the Parsee was kneeling in Ahab's front, but with his head bowed away from him; while nearby, from the arched and overhanging rigging, where they had just been engaged securing a spar, a number of the seamen, arrested by the glare, now gathered together and hung pendulous, like a cluster of wasps from a drooping, orchard bough. In various enchanted attitudes, like the standing or stepping or running skeletons in Herculaneum, others remained rooted to the deck; but all their eyes upcast.

"Aye, aye, men!" cried Ahab. "Look up at it; mark it well; the white flame but lights the way to the White Whale! Hand me those mainmast links there; I would fain feel this pulse, and let mine beat against it; blood against fire! So."

Then turning — the last link held fast in his left hand, he put his foot upon the Parsee; and with fixed upward eye and high-flung right arm, he stood erect before the lofty three-pointed trinity of flames.

"Oh! You clear spirit of clear fire, whom on these seas I as a Persian once did worship, till in the sacramental act so burned by you that to this hour I bear the scar; I now know you, clear spirit, and I now know that your right worship is defiance. To neither love nor reverence will you be kind; and even for hate you can but kill; and all are killed. No fearless fool now fronts you. I own your speechless, placeless power; but to the last gasp of my earthquake life will dispute its unconditional, unintegral mastery in me. In the midst of the personified impersonal, a personality stands here."
[Sudden, repeated flashes of lightning; the nine flames leap lengthwise to thrice their previous height; Ahab, with the rest, closes his eyes, his right hand pressed hard upon them.]

"I own your speechless, placeless power; said I not so? Nor was it wrung from me; nor do I now drop these links. You can blind; but I can then grope. You can consume; but I can then be ashes. Take the homage of these poor eyes, and shutter-hands. I would not take it. The lightning flashes through my skull; my eyeballs ache and ache; my whole beaten brain seems as beheaded, and rolling on some stunning ground. Oh, oh! Yet blindfold, yet will I talk to you. Light though you be, you leap out of darkness; but I am darkness leaping out of light, leaping out of you! Here I devoutly pledge myself to what I adore in you — and defiance to all else. Oh, you magnanimous! Now I do glory in my genealogy. But you are but my fiery father; my sweet mother, I know not. Oh, cruel! What have you done with her? There lies my puzzle; but yours is greater. You know not how you came, hence call yourself unbegun. I know that of me, which you know not of yourself, oh omnipotent. There is some unsuffusing thing beyond you, clear spirit, to whom all your eternity is but time, all your creativeness mechanical. Through you, your flaming self, my scorched eyes do dimly see it. Oh, you foundling fire, you hermit immemorial, you too have your incommunicable riddle, your unparticipated grief. Here again with haughty agony, I read my sire. Leap! Leap up, and lick the sky! I leap with you; I burn with you; would fain be welded with you; defiantly I worship you!"
"The boat! The boat!" cried Starbuck, "look at your boat, old man!"

Ahab's harpoon, the one forged at Perth's fire, remained firmly lashed in its conspicuous crotch, so that it projected beyond his whale-boat's bow; but the sea that had stove its bottom had caused the loose leather sheath to drop off; and from the keen steel barb there now came a leveled flame of pale, forked fire. As the silent harpoon burned there like a serpent's tongue, Starbuck grasped Ahab by the arm: "God, God is against you, old man; forbear! It is an ill voyage! Ill begun, ill continued; let me square the yards while we may, old man, and make a fair wind of it homeward, to go on a better voyage than this."

Overhearing Starbuck, the panic-stricken crew instantly ran to the braces — though not a sail was left aloft. For the moment all the aghast mate's thoughts seemed theirs; they raised a half-mutinous cry. But dashing the rattling lightning links to the deck, and snatching the burning harpoon, Ahab waved it like a torch among them; swearing to impale with it the first sailor that but cast loose a rope's end. Petrified by his desperate daring, and his wild words but still more desperate, the men fell back in dismay, and Ahab again spoke:

"All your oaths to hunt the White Whale are as binding as mine; and heart, soul, and body, lungs and life, old Ahab is bound. And that you may know to what tune this heart beats — look here; thus I blow out the last fear!" And with one blast of his breath he extinguished the flame.

As in the hurricane that sweeps the plain, men flee the neighborhood of some lone, gigantic elm, whose very height and strength but render it so much the more unsafe, because so much the more a mark for thunderbolts; so at those last words of Ahab's, many of the sailors did run from him in a terror of dismay.
